paragraphs: When data collection responds to earlier observations, ordinary regression intuition can become unreliable. The collection policy creates sequential dependence, and the resulting estimation biases can persist even with arbitrarily large amounts of data. This paper studies how to obtain reliable inference for linear models in that adaptive setting.

The proposed method, W-decorrelation, transforms the bias of an adaptive regression estimator into variance. This makes the tradeoff explicit: reducing systematic distortion can come at the cost of greater variability. The procedure requires only broad information about the collection policy, without needing exact policy knowledge or propensity scores describing its selection probabilities.

The authors bound the estimator’s bias and variance for finite samples and establish asymptotically correct confidence intervals through a new martingale central limit theorem. Experiments in multi-armed bandits and autoregressive time series demonstrate empirical benefits. Together, these results address both the accuracy of adaptive estimates and the reliability of the uncertainty statements attached to them.
icml-2018-accurate-inference-for-adaptiv.tldr: W-decorrelation trades adaptive regression bias for variance to support more reliable estimation and asymptotically correct confidence intervals.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether deep learning models on graphs remain reliable when an attacker changes the structure of their input. Its focus is the combinatorial arrangement of the data: structural modifications can cause a classifier to make a different prediction. The work examines this vulnerability for both classifying whole graphs and classifying individual nodes.

The authors develop attacks for different levels of access to the target model. A reinforcement learning approach learns a generalizable attack policy using only predicted labels. When richer information is available, they also propose methods based on genetic algorithms and gradient descent, using prediction confidence or gradients to guide the attack.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world data show that a family of graph neural networks is vulnerable to these methods. The findings establish weaknesses in the evaluated models and tasks, without implying that every graph classifier fails. The authors also show that attacks can help diagnose learned classifiers, making structural perturbations useful for examining model behavior as well as exposing errors.
icml-2018-adversarial-attack-on-graph-st.tldr: Structural attacks can fool graph neural networks, including through a learned attack policy that needs only prediction labels.

paragraphs: Ridge regression is useful when a dataset has many more predictor variables than observations, but finding its solution can involve a large design matrix. This paper proposes an iterative algorithm that uses sketching to obtain a high-quality approximation to the optimal coefficient vector. The central question is how much of the original problem must be retained to preserve accuracy.

The analysis rests on two structural results that reduce the essential reasoning to randomized matrix multiplication. A particularly important part concerns subsampling with ridge leverage scores. The authors prove that accurate approximations can use a sample size governed by the problem’s degrees of freedom rather than by the raw dimensions of its design matrix.

That distinction makes the guarantee sensitive to the regression problem’s effective complexity, rather than simply the number of entries describing it. The contribution combines an approximation algorithm with an explanation of why its sampling strategy can work. Evaluations on both real and synthetic datasets support the theoretical results.
icml-2018-an-iterative-sketching-based-f.tldr: An iterative sketching method approximates ridge regression with sampling guarantees tied to effective degrees of freedom rather than matrix dimensions.

paragraphs: Distributed training must sometimes handle workers that return corrupt updates because of faults, bad data, or malicious behavior. Asynchronous training adds another difficulty: updates can arrive after the model has already changed. This paper introduces Kardam, an asynchronous stochastic gradient descent algorithm designed to address both Byzantine workers and stale information.

Kardam combines filtering with dampening. Its scalar-based filter uses Lipschitz properties of the cost functions to resist corrupt updates, with stated resilience against one-third Byzantine workers. Its dampening component weights gradients to account for staleness. The authors prove almost sure convergence in the analyzed setting and derive a convergence rate.

Evaluations on CIFAR100 and EMNIST examine the cost of this resilience. The authors report no additional learning noise, while describing a slowdown bounded by less than f/n, where f is the tolerated failure count and n the worker count. They also find that dampening alone can outperform alternative staleness-aware asynchronous methods when workers are honest.
icml-2018-asynchronous-byzantine-machine.tldr: Kardam combines gradient filtering and staleness-aware weighting to support convergent asynchronous training despite Byzantine workers.

paragraphs: Pruning whole neurons can reduce a neural network’s stored size, arithmetic work, and memory use during execution. This paper develops a compression method that decides which neurons to preserve through the information bottleneck principle. The aim is to concentrate useful information in fewer neurons while reducing redundancy between neighboring layers.

The authors make this information-based objective tractable through a variational bound. Minimizing the bound encourages useful information to accumulate in a subset of neurons. Activations of neurons that can be discarded are suppressed through a form of sparse regularization that arises from the framework itself, rather than being added as a separate conventional sparsity penalty.

The paper reports advantages over traditional sparsity penalties without introducing additional tuning parameters into the objective landscape. Across multiple datasets and network architectures, the authors demonstrate compression rates described as state of the art. The significance is a principled connection between preserving information and removing neurons, with compression targeting several practical resource costs at once.
icml-2018-compressing-neural-networks-us.tldr: A variational information bottleneck concentrates useful information into fewer neurons, enabling strong network compression through pruning.

paragraphs: Selecting several useful groups requires more than making each group strong on its own. The groups may also need to avoid repeating one another’s information. This paper formalizes that problem using submodular scores for individual blocks, constraints specific to each block, and interaction scores that reward a collection of mutually nonredundant blocks.

The formulation captures diversity both within groups and between them. For the non-robust version, the authors reduce the task to non-monotone submodular maximization under multiple matroid constraints. For a version combining robust and average performance, they provide a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm with a bi-criterion guarantee and a randomized algorithm with a probabilistic guarantee.

Those latter guarantees require the relevant submodular functions, including the interaction terms, to be monotone. The framework has potential uses in model ensembles, parallel data processing, and summarization. A classifier-ensemble case study reports good results, illustrating how jointly selecting diverse groups can produce useful collections rather than merely several individually appealing choices.
icml-2018-constrained-interacting-submod.tldr: The paper develops algorithms for forming constrained groups that are valuable individually and diverse collectively, with guarantees for specified cases.

paragraphs: Uncertain predictions can reflect uncertainty about the model or noise in the observations themselves. This paper separates those sources using Bayesian neural networks with latent variables. Uncertainty in the network weights represents incomplete knowledge of the model, while latent variables allow the model to capture complex patterns of noise in the data.

The authors show how to decompose predictive uncertainty into epistemic and aleatoric components and use that distinction when choosing what to learn next. In active learning, they successfully identify informative points for functions with heteroscedastic noise, whose level varies, and bimodal noise. The decomposition makes the source of uncertainty relevant to the selection decision.

The paper also uses the same distinction to define a risk-sensitive reinforcement learning criterion. This criterion balances expected cost, model bias, and aversion to noise when identifying policies. Its contribution is to turn uncertainty into separate decision-relevant quantities, allowing learning and control choices to account for why an outcome is uncertain.
icml-2018-decomposition-of-uncertainty-i.tldr: Separating model uncertainty from data noise supports informative data selection and reinforcement learning policies that balance distinct sources of risk.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning agents can achieve strong performance while still requiring large amounts of experience. Building an environment model offers a way to make more use of what has already been observed, because planning can update decisions without relying only on new interactions. This paper introduces Variational State Tabulation, or VaST, to connect that strategy with high-dimensional observations.

VaST maps an environment’s large state space, such as visual inputs, into an abstract tabular model. That representation allows the agent to use prioritized sweeping with small backups to update state-action values. The approach connects learned state abstraction to an efficient planning method that operates on the resulting table.

The authors show that VaST can rapidly learn reward-maximizing behavior in tasks including 3D navigation. They also demonstrate efficient adaptation when rewards or transition probabilities change suddenly. These findings highlight two uses of the abstract model: learning from limited experience and revising behavior when previously learned environmental relationships or rewards change.
icml-2018-efficient-model-based-deep-rei.tldr: VaST converts high-dimensional observations into a tabular model that supports efficient planning and adaptation to environmental changes.

paragraphs: In nonconvex optimization, a saddle point can have directions of negative curvature even when the gradient provides little immediate guidance. Some methods inject random noise to help move away from such points. This paper asks whether the randomness already present in stochastic gradients can serve that purpose under a suitable condition.

The authors analyze certain machine learning models and find substantial stochastic-gradient variance along negative-curvature directions. That variance scales with the magnitude of the corresponding curvature eigenvalues and does not decrease with dimension. This differs from isotropic noise, whose randomness is spread without favoring those particular directions.

Motivated by this observation, the paper introduces an assumption under which a simple stochastic gradient step can replace explicit isotropic noise for escaping saddles. Under the same condition, it establishes a convergence rate for plain stochastic gradient descent to a second-order stationary point with an iteration count independent of problem dimension. The guarantee depends on the stated condition; it does not establish dimension-independent convergence for arbitrary stochastic gradients.
icml-2018-escaping-saddles-with-stochast.tldr: Under a proposed condition on stochastic-gradient noise, plain SGD can escape saddles and reach second-order stationarity with dimension-independent iteration complexity.

paragraphs: Continuous-action reinforcement learning can struggle when rewards are sparse or point exploration in an unhelpful direction. Gradient-based methods such as DDPG can refine policies, but their exploration may be inefficient in these settings. Exploration-oriented methods offer a complementary strength: they explore more robustly, while being less efficient at fine-tuning policies through gradient descent.

GEP-PG combines these capabilities sequentially. It first uses a Goal Exploration Process and then combines that exploration stage with DDPG-based policy improvement. The paper studies two DDPG variants, the exploration component, and their combinations to examine how separating exploration from later refinement affects learning.

The evaluations cover a low-dimensional problem with deceptive rewards and the larger Half-Cheetah benchmark. DDPG fails on the deceptive-reward problem, while GEP-PG improves over the best evaluated DDPG variant in both environments. These results support the value of the staged combination in the tested settings: better exploration can provide a more useful starting point for gradient-based policy refinement.
icml-2018-gep-pg-decoupling-exploration-.tldr: GEP-PG improves learning in two evaluated environments by combining goal-directed exploration with subsequent DDPG policy refinement.

paragraphs: An action can lead to a range of future returns, and a distributional reinforcement learning agent models that range. This paper develops a flexible distributional version of DQN by learning the return distribution through its quantile function. A quantile describes the return associated with a particular position in that distribution.

The method uses quantile regression to approximate the full quantile function for each state-action return distribution. Reparameterizing a distribution over the sample space then defines the return distribution implicitly. This representation also supports a large class of risk-sensitive policies, making the learned distribution useful for more than a single expected-return estimate.

The authors demonstrate improved performance across the evaluation involving 57 Atari 2600 games in the Arcade Learning Environment. They also use the implicitly represented distributions to investigate the effects of risk-sensitive policies in those games. The contribution links a flexible way to represent uncertain returns with practical policy choices about how those returns should influence action selection.
icml-2018-implicit-quantile-networks-for.tldr: Implicit Quantile Networks learn return distributions through quantile regression, improving Atari performance and enabling varied risk-sensitive policies.

paragraphs: Variational autoencoders use a recognition network to produce an approximate posterior for each datapoint, making inference scalable across large datasets. Approximation quality depends on two separate capabilities: whether the chosen distribution family can represent the true posterior, and whether the recognition network can find good parameters within that family. This paper examines those contributions separately.

The authors find that imperfect recognition networks often account for divergence from the true posterior more than limited distributional complexity does. They also show that this outcome partly reflects adaptation by the generator: during learning, it can accommodate the chosen form of approximation. The inference problem and the learned generative model therefore influence one another.

Another finding concerns parameters added to make the approximation more expressive. Their value includes helping inference generalize, rather than only expanding the range of distributions that can be represented. The study shows why improving inference requires attention to both representation capacity and the network that selects approximate-posterior parameters for individual observations.
icml-2018-inference-suboptimality-in-var.tldr: VAE inference errors often arise from imperfect recognition networks, while added expressiveness can help inference generalize as well as represent richer posteriors.

paragraphs: Many graph algorithms repeatedly update quantities until they reach a steady state. The desired solution can often be described by fixed-point conditions: relationships that hold once further updates no longer change the result. This paper investigates learning an algorithm from examples while retaining those conditions as a guide to the intended solution.

The authors propose an embedding representation for iterative graph algorithms. Their learning procedure alternates between updating the embeddings and projecting them onto steady-state constraints. This couples learning from examples with the mathematical relationships that characterize the output of the underlying graph computation.

The framework is evaluated using several commonly used graph algorithms. The authors demonstrate effectiveness and report that, in some cases, a learned algorithm can handle graphs exceeding 100 million nodes on one machine. That scale result is explicitly case-dependent. The broader contribution is a way to combine learned representations with fixed-point structure, connecting data-driven algorithm learning to the steady-state solutions that graph analytics seeks.
icml-2018-learning-steady-states-of-iter.tldr: A learned embedding framework uses steady-state constraints to solve graph problems, reaching graphs above 100 million nodes in some evaluated cases.

paragraphs: Gibbs sampling can become expensive on graphical models where each variable is connected to many factors. Even one update may require work proportional to the number of adjacent factors. This paper targets that local computational bottleneck, asking whether an update can use a sampled subset of factors while preserving useful sampling guarantees.

The proposed approach uses minibatches to estimate the sum of factor contributions. The authors introduce several Gibbs variants based on this idea and show that they can be made unbiased. They also establish bounds on convergence rates, addressing how the modified update mechanism affects the progress of the sampling procedure.

Under some conditions, the variants achieve asymptotic speedups in the runtime of a single update compared with ordinary Gibbs sampling. The result is specifically about per-update cost, while the convergence analysis addresses a separate part of overall sampling behavior. Together, the contributions provide a theoretical basis for reducing work in densely connected graphical models without treating subsampling as an unexamined approximation.
icml-2018-minibatch-gibbs-sampling-on-la.tldr: Minibatched Gibbs variants subsample factors, can be made unbiased, and offer faster individual updates under specified conditions.

paragraphs: Some reinforcement learning agents are difficult to train because their policy representations are complex from the outset. Mix and Match addresses this by constructing a curriculum over agents themselves. It progressively trains more complex agents using solutions discovered by simpler ones, allowing earlier learning to support later stages of training.

The curriculum changes how the policy is represented internally, rather than gradually changing the tasks or environments. The framework can progress through action spaces or through architectural variants that define an agent’s internal state. This makes agent design part of the training progression instead of fixing its full complexity at the beginning.

The authors report significant performance gains in three experimental setups. In a challenging 3D first-person task with more than 700 actions, an action-space curriculum produces faster training and better final performance than traditional methods. They also demonstrate successful architectural curricula and a variant that improves multitask performance. These examples support the framework’s applicability across several forms of agent complexity.
icml-2018-mix-match-agent-curricula-for-.tldr: Mix and Match trains increasingly complex reinforcement learning agents by building on simpler agents through curricula over policy representations.

paragraphs: Accelerated optimization methods are attractive because they converge quickly across many large-scale problems. Their behavior becomes harder to understand when the supplied gradients contain noise or other inaccuracies. This paper studies how acceleration interacts with those imperfect gradient signals, treating stability as a central part of evaluating an optimization method.

The authors introduce AGDP, an accelerated algorithm that generalizes Nesterov’s accelerated gradient descent and improves on AXGD. Its comparatively simple form and analysis provide a basis for examining noisy and inexact gradient oracles. The algorithm is therefore both a methodological contribution and a vehicle for understanding acceleration under imperfect information.

The theoretical study is supported by numerical experiments. It also motivates modifications intended to reduce both the mean and variance of the error caused by gradient noise. These two targets address the average magnitude of noise-related error and its variability. The findings clarify how accelerated methods can be adjusted in noisy settings, without claiming that acceleration is universally insensitive to gradient corruption.
icml-2018-on-acceleration-with-noise-cor.tldr: AGDP provides a new accelerated optimization method and an analysis that motivates reducing the average and variability of errors from noisy gradients.

paragraphs: An online learner may sometimes prefer to withhold a prediction, provided it pays a specified cost. That option changes the learning problem because abstaining becomes part of the learner’s decision process. This paper studies how to learn effectively with this choice in both adversarial and stochastic settings.

For the adversarial case, the authors show how to adapt existing online algorithms and their guarantees. In the stochastic case, they identify a bias problem that limits a straightforward extension of UCB-N. They then introduce UCB-GT, which uses historical data and feedback graphs that change over time to address this setting.

UCB-GT has more favorable regret guarantees than the natural UCB-N extension examined in the paper. Experiments also show that it substantially outperforms that extension and other standard baselines. The work connects a practical prediction option—declining to answer at a cost—with the statistical consequences of the available feedback, showing why an apparently direct algorithmic adaptation can require a more careful treatment.
icml-2018-online-learning-with-abstentio.tldr: UCB-GT uses historical data and changing feedback graphs to improve learning guarantees and empirical performance when predictions can be withheld at a cost.

paragraphs: This paper studies control when the system’s linear dynamics are known and do not change over time, but include noise. The costs are quadratic and may be chosen adversarially. A controller must therefore make sequential decisions in a setting where the physical dynamics are specified but the sequence of losses can be unfavorable.

The authors develop efficient online learning algorithms with regret bounded on the order of the square root of the time horizon, under mild assumptions. Such a bound means that the regret accumulated per step decreases as the horizon grows. The result concerns learning performance across the sequence of control decisions.

The algorithms rely on a new semidefinite programming relaxation describing the system’s steady-state distribution. A crucial property is that every feasible solution corresponds to a strongly stable policy, with exponential convergence toward a steady state. This connects the optimization representation to the behavior of the resulting controller: feasibility carries a stability property needed by the approach.
icml-2018-online-linear-quadratic-contro.tldr: A steady-state optimization relaxation yields efficient online controllers with square-root regret guarantees under mild assumptions and known noisy linear dynamics.

paragraphs: Entropy regularization influences how a reinforcement learning policy distributes probability among actions. Standard Shannon regularization produces softmax policies that may retain meaningful probability on non-optimal actions, especially with many available actions. This paper studies a Tsallis-entropy formulation whose optimal policy assigns nonzero probability to only a small subset of actions at each state.

The authors derive a sparse consistency equation connecting the optimal value function and policy along a trajectory. They also establish a weaker converse: satisfying the consistency relationship supports a quantified suboptimality result, rather than automatically implying exact optimality. This relationship supplies the basis for sparse path consistency learning algorithms that can use both on-policy and off-policy data.

The analysis shows a better suboptimality comparison with the soft-regularized optimal policy as the number of actions increases. Empirical comparisons likewise favor sparse PCL, particularly in problems with large action sets. The contribution connects sparse action selection to both a trajectory-based learning rule and an explicit analysis of the quality of consistent policies.
icml-2018-path-consistency-learning-in-t.tldr: Sparse PCL uses Tsallis entropy and trajectory consistency to learn sparse policies, with theoretical and empirical advantages especially for large action sets.

paragraphs: Function approximation makes reinforcement learning applicable beyond small tables, but it can undermine the stability of Bellman-based updates. The Bellman operator may become expansive, allowing errors to grow and causing methods such as Q-learning to oscillate or diverge. This paper tackles that difficulty by changing the mathematical formulation used for learning.

The authors reformulate the Bellman optimality equation as a primal-dual optimization problem using Nesterov smoothing and the Legendre-Fenchel transformation. They then develop Smoothed Bellman Error Embedding, or SBEED, to solve the resulting problem. The framework permits any differentiable function class, making nonlinear approximators part of the formulation rather than a special case excluded from it.

The paper provides a convergence guarantee for general nonlinear function approximation, described by the authors as a first to their knowledge, and analyzes sample complexity. On several benchmark control problems, SBEED compares favorably with leading baselines. The contribution combines an optimization reformulation, theoretical convergence analysis, and empirical evidence about its usefulness for control.
icml-2018-sbeed-convergent-reinforcement.tldr: SBEED reformulates Bellman learning as a smoothed primal-dual problem with convergence analysis for differentiable nonlinear function approximation.

paragraphs: Hierarchical reinforcement learning needs representations of behavior that extend across multiple steps. This paper approaches that need by learning continuous latent representations of whole trajectories. Its model, SeCTAR, draws on variational autoencoders and turns the learning of lower-level behavior into a trajectory-level generative modeling problem.

The central mechanism pairs a latent-conditioned policy with a latent-conditioned predictive model. Given the same latent representation, the policy should produce a trajectory matching the model’s prediction. This consistency gives the hierarchy a way to predict the outcome of executing a closed-loop policy, connecting its abstract choices to the behavior those choices should generate.

The authors combine planning in the learned latent space with an unsupervised exploration objective. Across several simulated tasks with sparse rewards, the method supports reasoning over long horizons and outperforms the evaluated standard reinforcement learning and prior hierarchical, planning, and exploration methods. The findings show how jointly learning behavior and its predicted outcome can support temporally extended, multistage decisions.
icml-2018-self-consistent-trajectory-aut.tldr: SeCTAR learns matching trajectory policies and predictions in a latent space to support hierarchical planning on long-horizon, sparse-reward tasks.

paragraphs: Predicting future video frames involves uncertainty about what will happen next. A useful generator must capture variation in possible outcomes while maintaining sharp images. This paper addresses both goals with a model that combines a deterministic prediction of a future frame with stochastic latent variables sampled at each time step.

The distribution used to sample those latent variables is learned. Drawing from this prior supplies a stochastic contribution to frame generation, which is combined with the deterministic estimate. The design gives the model an explicit mechanism for producing different future continuations while retaining a deterministic component in its predictions.

The authors describe the approach as simple and trainable end to end across a variety of datasets. They report generated sequences that remain both varied and sharp many frames into the future, with favorable comparisons to existing approaches. These observations support the learned-prior design as a way to represent uncertainty in video generation while preserving visual detail over longer predictions.
icml-2018-stochastic-video-generation-wi.tldr: A learned prior supplies time-step-specific randomness that helps a video generator produce varied, sharp future sequences.

paragraphs: A Wasserstein barycenter summarizes a collection of probability distributions using the geometry of optimal transport. Computing that representative distribution requires deciding both how to place its probability mass and where that mass can be located. This paper introduces a stochastic algorithm that can work with continuous input distributions.

A central feature is that the barycenter’s support—the locations where it places mass—can change at every iteration. The method also solves the problem without regularization. The authors state that this allows recovery of a sharp output whose support is contained in that of the true barycenter, tying the output’s locations to the target distribution’s support.

Examples show cases where the algorithm produces a more meaningful barycenter than previous approaches. The paper also describes extensions for generating super samples from a distribution and recovering blue-noise approximations. These applications illustrate the method’s versatility, while the main contribution is a barycenter computation procedure that accommodates continuous inputs and an adjustable support.
icml-2018-stochastic-wasserstein-barycen.tldr: A stochastic, unregularized algorithm computes Wasserstein barycenters with continuous inputs and support that can adapt during optimization.

paragraphs: Black-box policy optimization must estimate useful search directions without directly differentiating the objective. This paper proposes a gradient approximation method based on structured random orthogonal matrices. The authors provide theoretical guarantees and report more accurate estimators than the baselines, then apply the method to learning compact neural-network policies.

Compact policies reduce the resources required for both training and inference, making them relevant to hardware with limited capacity. They also provide architectures that scale better for derivative-free optimization in high-dimensional spaces. The paper reports learning better-quality compact policies than those obtained using standard gradient estimation techniques.

For most robotics tasks in OpenAI Gym, the authors show solutions using networks with fewer than 300 parameters and inference complexity that is nearly linear. They report up to 13 times fewer parameters than the referenced Evolution Strategies approach. Good policies are learned without fitness-shaping heuristics. Together, the results connect a theoretically motivated estimator to small policy architectures with practical computational benefits.
icml-2018-structured-evolution-with-comp.tldr: Structured orthogonal gradient estimates enable effective black-box training of compact policies with lower parameter counts and efficient inference.

paragraphs: Recovering a hidden network from observations requires deciding which parts of the signal should be attributed to network relationships. Traditional approaches can assume that the network explains all signal, or constrain network parameters to secure stability. This paper develops a model that explicitly allows a separate source of signal outside the network.

The model places a Gaussian process prior on that network-independent component. This gives the inference procedure a way to represent variation without assigning all of it to the latent network. The authors formally establish algorithmic stability without the stabilizing parameter restrictions that motivate their critique of earlier methods.

The paper also presents a new perspective on model stability, robustness results, and precise intervals for key inference parameters. These contributions address both how the inference procedure behaves and how its inferred quantities can be characterized. Across three applications, the proposed approach consistently outperforms previous methods. The findings support separating network-related signal from other variation as a useful modeling choice for latent-network discovery.
icml-2018-variational-network-inference-.tldr: A latent-network model with a Gaussian-process component for outside signal provides stability and robustness results and improves performance on three applications.
